entries.title: Espionage, true crime and war: Baillie Gifford longlist revealed
entries.summary: Patrick Radden Keefe, Ben Macintyre and the Guardian’s Charlotte Higgins are among the 13 authors selected for the nonfiction awardThe Guardian’s chief culture writer Charlotte Higgins joins American investigative journalist Patrick Radden Keefe and bestselling historian Ben Macintyre on this year’s Baillie Gifford prize longlist.Higgins’ book, Ukrainian Lessons: Art in a Time of War, examines the
entries.content:
The Guardian’s chief culture writer Charlotte Higgins joins American investigative journalist Patrick Radden Keefe and bestselling historian Ben Macintyre on this year’s Baillie Gifford prize longlist.

Higgins’ book, Ukrainian Lessons: Art in a Time of War, examines the role of culture in Ukraine’s resistance to Russia’s invasion, drawing on multiple reporting trips to Ukraine. Keefe, who won the prize in 2021 with Empire of Pain, is listed again for London Falling, which tells the story of Zac Brettler, a teenager who fell from a luxury London apartment after having posed as the son of a wealthy Russian oligarch. Macintyre’s Redwood: The Untold Story of the Cold War’s Most Extraordinary Spy, tells the story of a KGB double agent cultivated by MI6 in revolutionary Tehran.

The 13 books on the longlist, selected from submissions published in English in the UK over the past year, range from biography and ancient history to espionage, true crime and international reportage. The prize is widely regarded as the UK’s most prestigious award for nonfiction.

“Chairing this prize is like being part of a very well-informed and opinionated book group,” said lead judge Kirsty Lang. “Whittling our choices down to 13 books led to some forthright discussion, but we got there in the end and are very proud of our longlist.”

Biography is a major theme of this year’s list. In Baldwin: A Love Story, the first major study of James Baldwin in 30 years, Nicholas Boggs examines Baldwin’s relationships and their influence on his writing, drawing on previously unseen material and interviews.

The life of another literary figure is explored in The Great Dictator by Matthew Sweet. Sweet’s account of the romance novelist Barbara Cartland’s career is set against the backdrop of the changing sexual and social politics of her era. Meanwhile, Andrea Wulf’s The Traveller examines the largely forgotten 18th-century explorer George Forster, who joined Captain Cook’s second voyage around the world as a teenager.

Contemporary conflicts also loom large. In Days of Love and Rage, Anand Gopal reports from Manbij, Syria, during the revolution, telling the stories of people who helped overthrow a dictatorship. The Bookseller of Kabul author Åsne Seierstad offers an account of contemporary Russia in Never Say War; while Ian Buruma’s Stay Alive: Berlin, 1939–1945 examines how ordinary people navigated life under the Nazi regime. Ancient history is represented by Edmund Richardson’s Alexander: God, King, Man, a portrait of Alexander the Great.

In The Nord Stream Conspiracy the Wall Street Journal political correspondent Bojan Pancevski probes the sabotage of North Sea gas pipelines. While Murder in Paris ’68 by Edward Chisholm revisits one of French cinema’s most notorious scandals: the murder of actor Alain Delon’s bodyguard, Stefan Marković.

Completing this year’s longlist, Jane Rogoyska’s Hotel Exile tells the wartime story of the Hôtel Lutetia in Paris which was transformed from a gathering place for refugee artists, activists and intellectuals into the headquarters of Nazi intelligence.

The longlist was selected by Lang, Waterstones’s head of books Bea Carvalho, writer and cultural historian Tiffany Jenkins, Spectator literary editor Sam Leith, editor and reporter Ravi Mattu and novelist Elif Shafak.

The prize, established as the Samuel Johnson prize in 1999, has been sponsored by Edinburgh-based investment management firm Baillie Gifford since 2016. The company has faced criticism in recent years over its investments in fossil fuels and companies with links to Israel. In 2024, campaign group Fossil Free Books organised boycotts of literary festivals sponsored by the firm, resulting in Baillie Gifford ending its partnerships with nine festivals.

The winner will receive £50,000, with the shortlist of six announced on 1 October and the winner on 4 November. Last year’s prize was won by Australian writer Helen Garner for How to End a Story: Collected Diaries.

Browse all the books on the Baillie Gifford 2025 longlist at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

entries.title: A Death of One’s Own by Terry Eagleton review – meditations on arriving at a full stop
entries.summary: The literary critic brings his vast reading to bear on life’s most inescapable factTerry Eagleton is not a fan of sloppy thinking, especially when it comes to the granite fact of death. entries.content:
Terry Eagleton is not a fan of sloppy thinking, especially when it comes to the granite fact of death. He particularly doesn’t like the attitude of Dylan Thomas who famously urged his ailing father to “not go gentle into that good night”. If the “night” – death – is so “good” then why, asks Eagleton reasonably, would Thomas want his dad to dawdle? Shouldn’t DJ Thomas, rather, be encouraged to trot towards his lovely end like an ecstatic marathon runner on the home straight?

Eagleton’s reproach to Thomas’s doublethink should not be read as panicky denial about the reality of his own mortality. To the contrary, Eagleton, who at 83 admits that he wasn’t sure whether this book would end up being published posthumously, finds it hard to think or write about much else. After a 60-year academic career spent tussling with Marxist literary theory, not to mention the epistemological void at the heart of postmodernism criticism, these days Eagleton is more interested in pondering death and how it “lacks a sense of occasion”. It might visit, for example, while you happen to be dressed in a giraffe outfit.

Not, Eagleton clarifies, that it would really matter being found dead disguised as a long-necked ungulate since you would be beyond all caring. Indeed, this not mattering is, as he sees it, one of the great pleasures of being deceased. You’re beyond the reach of moral and social obligation: you can cheat your creditors, fail to turn up at your mother’s funeral and ignore increasingly hysterical demands to pay a parking fine. There might even be something sexy about being dead, a certain “pornographic pleasure” in decomposition, what Eagleton calls “the erotic bliss of yielding to an impregnable power”. Practically speaking, you’re no longer required to hold it all together.

Until that moment of blessed release, though, we are obliged to trundle on as best we can. Eagleton mildly advocates trying to live each day in the full knowledge that death is just around the corner. Done right, this should in theory release us “from the mortal anxiety that compels us to clutch, seize and despoil”. Instead, we would experience the world around us with the visionary intensity of a William Blake, savouring every raindrop, ray of sunlight and crunch of apple to the point of almost painful lucidity. Lovely in principle, but as Eagleton puts it with a typically bathetic side-swipe, the mental contortion required to attain this state of ecstasy may end up being “more trouble than it’s worth”.

For the fact remains that we are time-trapped creatures, forever casting back to the past and projecting forward to an imagined future, refusing to live in the reality of now. For this reason, our meagre deaths tend to arrive like an unexpected insult, a monstrous unfairness that we weren’t expecting. Eagleton is consoling here about the fact that when death arrives we probably won’t say the right or splendid thing. Thomas’s final words were apparently “the End is in Eden” which, as Eagleton tartly points out, is just one more of the old windbag’s “metaphysical vacuities”.

As far as deathbed utterance goes, better instead to recall Steve Jobs’s less prescriptive “Oh wow. Oh wow. Oh wow”, which doesn’t strain for “sham grandeur” and leaves the listener free to fill in the blank according to their own fantasies. Personally, I’ve always liked to imagine that Jobs was being shown a vision of a heavenly Apple store, with serried ranks of angels in cobalt-coloured T-shirts tip-tapping away on futuristic Macs.

A Death of One’s Own is in no sense an argument about its subject or even a sustained inquiry into death’s terrors and odd consolations. Instead, Eagleton lets his capacious mind, vast reading and wicked wit loose over the whole business of arriving at a full stop. In his introduction he explains that he has included ideas and individuals that have been central to his “spiritual and intellectual life” of the past six decades. Marx, Freud and cradle Catholicism are all invited to troop on stage to take a final bow “before the curtain comes down”. I found that the best way to read this book, which is undeniably dense, is to take in a bit each night before going to sleep, that “little death” from which, God willing, we awake refreshed each morning.

entries.title: The Bridge by Colm Tóibín review – betrayal and survival in the High Pyrenees
entries.summary: Deep sorrow mingles with illicit desire in this potent novella, the follow-up to a 2006 story about an isolated family in the Catalan mountainsTwenty years ago, Colm Tóibín published a steadily desolating novella set in the high villages of the Catalan Pyrenees. A woman walks out of her house and her life, starts along the mountain road and disappears in the snow. Her son Miquel, failing to find h
entries.content:
Twenty years ago, Colm Tóibín published a steadily desolating novella set in the high villages of the Catalan Pyrenees. A woman walks out of her house and her life, starts along the mountain road and disappears in the snow. Her son Miquel, failing to find her body, waits through the dark months for the thaw. A Long Winter, which appeared in a standalone volume and then as the final story in the 2006 collection Mothers and Sons, followed Miquel through dramatically extreme circumstances and patient endurance. It was told with the most restrained prose ever likely to be employed for a son’s view of vultures circling a corpse.

Now, in The Bridge, a single year has passed in Miquel’s life and he is eking out an existence with his hurtful, unyielding father. The sheep are grazing their high summer pastures; a side hustle smuggling contraband brings in a little much-needed cash. In the bare conditions of the lonely farm, any warmth of feeling is a kind of contraband smuggled in by night; love between men is doubly illicit. The grave tenderness that grows between Miquel and his father’s maltreated servant Manolo gives The Bridge its emotional centre. These young men salve the emptiness with a few quiet words and touches. We sense their youthful beauty and resilience, their suppleness in a place of fixity.

In fact, and with a fullness that’s striking in this novella of watchfulness and withholding, Miquel enters into a varied erotic life. Visits to the local town bring assignations. A later relationship between cellmates is extraordinarily vivid as Miquel seeks to “assuage his hunger by biting Odo, chewing him”. But it’s the lost, interrupted love of Manolo that gives shape to the rest.

A great alteration has come to the area in the form of a road bridge linking isolated settlements with the country beyond. Places “cut off and enclosed” for centuries are suddenly opened and connected. This central motif suggests a story concerned with social change, and certainly it could be described in those terms. There’s a potent scene in which dogs from both sides of the valley run wildly across the bridge, frenzied at the possibility of new mates. This is not the only moment of the feral, and the farcical. As for Miquel: the crossing should bring him a larger terrain for youthful exploration, but it casts him into peril and dire confinement. The Bridge stays in the mind less as a historically specific story of 20th-century development than as an ageless study of loss, betrayal and survival. Miquel himself comes to believe that “his isolation was nothing new, that he had always been far away even from those to whom he had been closest”.

Tóibín’s relationship with Catalonia now spans five decades. His first novel was set in Barcelona; his latest collection, The News from Dublin, includes several fine Spanish stories. He spends part of each year in the mountains near Llavorsí, and in writing about Miquel he is thinking his way into lives that have unfolded in that long known yet hardly knowable place. The germ of Miquel’s story came in a particular glimpse of local history. Tóibín was told that a ruined building was all that remained of the house where a woman once grew desperate enough to walk away from her family. It was said that the snow came; it was said to be a terrible tale. A Long Winter and The Bridge have grown from that beginning.

Tóibín responds powerfully to the qualities of exactitude and seriousness he finds in Catalan writing, in the work of Mercè Rodereda for instance, and these are very much qualities of The Bridge. We know that Miquel feels deeply, but nothing in his life has licensed or recommended the articulation of personal emotion. Tóibín practises a sustained reticence, even as fate strikes so cruelly as to give this story an absurdist edge.

Readers of Brooklyn and its follow-up Long Island will know that Tóibín has careful ways of handling a sequel: those novels are both richly complete in themselves while opening depths in each other. The Bridge, too, works alone or as part of a pair. To read A Long Winter afterwards, meeting the past that crouches in the shadows of the later story, would be as absorbing as to read chronologically. A further instalment seems possible. Any change would be welcome to lift Miquel from stultifying conditions, though it’s unlikely to offer much relief.

This is the kind of small volume temptingly piled by the checkouts at Christmas. I wouldn’t recommend it as a stocking-filler; the stocking would fall to the floor with the weight of sorrow. But this is a memorable short work in which Tóibín’s unsentimental prose is flawlessly matched to the austere worlds of people enduring, in their different ways, lives stripped back to the bone.

The Bridge by Colm Tóibín is published by Picador (£12.99). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

entries.title: Profits, Prophets, Coaches and Kings by Jared Diamond review – how to change the course of history
entries.summary: The author of Guns, Germs and Steel falters in this flawed study of whether individuals really make a differenceEarly in this book, Jared Diamond proudly introduces “what I term ‘the Hamlet test’”, which helps decide whether prominent individuals really make a difference, or whether others might have done just as well. Among William Shakespeare’s contemporaries on the Elizabethan stage, he explain
entries.content:
Early in this book, Jared Diamond proudly introduces “what I term ‘the Hamlet test’”, which helps decide whether prominent individuals really make a difference, or whether others might have done just as well. Among William Shakespeare’s contemporaries on the Elizabethan stage, he explains, were “Ben Jonson, Christopher Marlowe and John Webster. But not even their best plays remotely approach in quality Hamlet and Shakespeare’s other masterpieces.” It follows, for Diamond, that Shakespeare was indeed “uniquely talented”: “We can be confident that no Elizabethan other than Shakespeare could have written a masterpiece like Hamlet if Shakespeare hadn’t done so.”

One obvious problem with this is that Marlowe was stabbed to death in a pub in Deptford in 1593 at the age of 29, having already written the absolute bangers Doctor Faustus and Tamburlaine, as well as – so it is now thought – co-writing the Henry VI trilogy with the up-and-coming Shakespeare. Shakespeare himself did not begin to compose his major tragedies, including Hamlet, until he was a decade older. So we can’t rule out the possibility that, had Marlowe lived another 10 years, he would have matched or even exceeded his colleague’s genius. Scholars widely agree that Hamlet and Shakespeare’s other masterpieces were possible only thanks to the outsized influence of Marlowe.

But Diamond is not interested in what literary scholars think, and is confident that his “Hamlet test” is a fine intellectual novelty. Indeed, he is not much interested in what scholars of history, or ethics, or business studies think either, because this is one of those books that pretends the subject is one nobody has thought rigorously about before.

Diamond argues persuasively that at least the first president of independent Botswana, Seretse Khama, passes the Hamlet test: he made the country safe for democracy by “gut[ting] the power of the traditional chiefs”, for example, but only he could do that, “because he was the most powerful chief”. Much later in the book, we happily agree that only a particular couple of very rich Californians could have invented the pomegranate-juice industry – or, to generalise the lesson, you have to have lots of wealth already to go into a business with very high up-front costs and a lengthy startup period. No shit, Sherlock, as the reader will have cause to exclaim at numerous points throughout the book.

As Diamond skips from politics to sport to business, the main interest is supplied by his concentration on the method of “natural experiments”: the statistical comparison of similar past events. In the 1990s, economists David Card and Alan Krueger analysed fast-food joints close together on either side of a state line: New Jersey had just passed a law to increase its minimum wage, while its neighbour Pennsylvania had not. In two celebrated papers, they proved that the increase in the minimum wage led to higher employment, contrary to the received economic wisdom. Similar analyses suggest that CEOs are responsible for between 6% and 29% of the variation in a company’s earnings, while sports coaches are on the hook for at most about 30% of a team’s performance. (Here I thought I could hear Thomas Tuchel breathing a sigh of relief.)

Analysis of natural experiments is a fun tool, but obviously harder to make work the further you travel from objectively quantifiable things such as money or win/loss records. One Diamond cites used the amount of parking fines incurred by national staff at the UN’s New York headquarters as a proxy for their countries’ level of political corruption, which is already a stretch. Another took the preponderance of cousin marriage as a proxy for lower IQ (because of inbreeding effects), and so found that stupider European monarchs over the past four centuries were less successful in expanding their territory. (Not supplied here is any argument that expanding your territory is always good.)

One of Diamond’s more striking examples also betrays some unreliability on his part. He writes that in their 2009 paper Hit or Miss? The Effect of Assassinations on Institutions and War, Benjamin F Jones and Benjamin A Olken showed that successful assassinations don’t make much difference to the outbreak of wars, and concludes that the killing of Franz Ferdinand didn’t cause the first world war. But the study itself explicitly cautions against that inference: Ferdinand is not included in their data, since he was not the “leader” of the Austro-Hungarian empire. Diamond also neglects to mention that paper’s more interesting finding, which is that, in autocracies, assassination can help make a transition to democracy more likely.

The book ends by suggesting other questions that “natural experiments” of this kind might address, on the implicit grounds that only quantitative methods from the social sciences can provide satisfactory answers. One of them is “Under what circumstances do military leaders most make a difference?” On this topic, Diamond might have read with profit a book by a military historian, for example, Lawrence Freedman’s superbCommand. But from this book’s Olympian perspective, subject-matter experts in military affairs are as invisible as those in literary history.

entries.title: Anita Brookner by Hermione Lee review – an enigmatic literary great given her due
entries.summary: This exhaustive biography of the Booker winner brings her properly out of the shadows for the first time‘Dr Weiss, at forty, knew that her life had been ruined by literature.” The first fictional sentence Anita Brookner ever published, aged 53, in A Start in Life, certainly set a tone. If people have heard of Brookner today, Hermione Lee says, they imagine a lonely, cardiganed woman yearning for a
entries.content:
‘Dr Weiss, at forty, knew that her life had been ruined by literature.” The first fictional sentence Anita Brookner ever published, aged 53, in A Start in Life, certainly set a tone. If people have heard of Brookner today, Hermione Lee says, they imagine a lonely, cardiganed woman yearning for an absent lover. “This,” says Lee (an emeritus English professor at the University of Oxford), “won’t do.”

The cardiganed image confuses the author with her protagonists. Of 24 novels written across 30 years, only the first four – A Start in Life, Providence, Look at Me and Hotel du Lac – are about a single woman pining for love. There is certainly a “Brooknerian” style, characterised by elegance, restraint and melancholia, but her fiction engaged with our emotional lives broadly, examining family, exile, home, trauma, ageing and much more.

Born in 1928 and raised in south London by a fearsome Polish-Jewish grandmother and absurdly ineffectual parents (a tobacco salesman and a failed singer), Brookner was a highly academic only child. After a degree at King’s College London, she briefly tasted freedom as a student in Paris, but was soon dragged back to care for her extraordinarily needy mother. Yoked to home for the next decade, she managed, nevertheless, to become a brilliant art critic and a charismatic lecturer at the Courtauld Institute, where she stayed until retirement.

In the introduction, Lee describes hearing the author’s voice saying, repeatedly, “Go away”, and Brookner’s 20s and 30s were the “most hidden, the least witnessed” of all. Brookner did her utmost to erase her life, and Lee is forced, therefore, to mine any detail she can find. As well as Brookner’s academic work and extensive reading habits, we get her poor handwriting, fear of trains, love of perfumes and at one particularly desperate point, salary increases over two decades. A couple of love affairs in her 30s fizzled out, but if there was ever a record of her feelings, Brookner expunged it. The first 200 pages, then, can be hard going. She was, says Lee, through gritted teeth, “an object of mystery and puzzlement”.

But Lee persists – always rake thin, Brookner kept slimming biscuits in her handbag; she loved babies; she doled out tranquillisers to nervous PhD candidates – and just as this enterprise starts to feel doomed, something miraculous happens. The tireless details begin to cohere and Brookner steps out of the shadows, intriguing, contradictory – the super brain who shaved 10 years off her age in her own Who’s Who entry; the self-proclaimed “loneliest woman in London” who had loads of friends.

The older she gets, the more interesting this book becomes. In 1979, her beloved Courtauld mentor, friend and boss, Anthony Blunt, was exposed as a Soviet spy. Shaken, Brookner remained loyal until she discovered he’d used her to extract information from a hospitalised colleague.

Reeling and depressed, facing another lonely summer, she found herself writing fiction. Her process was extraordinary. Each novel took only three months from start to finish. She’d roam London forming sentences in her head, then simply write them down, at speed. Hilary Mantel, a fervent admirer, said Brookner arrived as a novelist perfectly formed, “as if she had hatched from a marbled egg”. She would repeat this process, annually, for more than two decades.

In 1984, her fourth novel, Hotel du Lac, about a woman who jilts her fiancee and retreats to a Swiss hotel, won the Booker prize. Pretty much everyone expected JG Ballard’s Empire of the Sun or Julian Barnes’s Flaubert’s Parrot to win. The misogyny was mind-bending. At the ceremony, Ballard hissed, “You stole my Booker.” Private Eye snarked about “Hotel du Lac of Interest” and a grim pattern of critical disdain was set. For the rest of Brookner’s writing life, critics would carp about “doily” novels and compare her to Mills & Boon. Profiles were invariably illustrated with sad spinsters holding cups of tea. It tormented her. But she kept on writing.

She was, personally, far from isolated. She had devoted friends, including the Virago publisher Carmen Callil and fellow writers such as Rosamond Lehmann or Julian Barnes, who offers loving memories here. He was so intimidated by her eloquence when they lunched that he’d feel himself inserting semicolons into his own speech.

Was she a literary genius? She once, brilliantly, described novel-writing as “trying very hard to remember something which has not yet taken place”. Lee offers genuinely transporting literary criticism, unearthing the elegance and complexity of the work, but admits the compulsive production of a book a year diluted the impact and sometimes the quality. Still, she singles out three – Family and Friends, Latecomers and The Next Big Thing – as truly “outstanding” novels. Thankfully, it is no longer cool to Brookner-bash. This astute and tireless biography succeeds, against the odds, in unearthing the author – who would be appalled by our scrutiny. Above all, it shows that the work deserves our full attention.

entries.title: Emily Wilson to retranslate the Odyssey from scratch
entries.summary: Wilson, whose 2017 English translation of Homer’s epic poem inspired Christopher Nolan’s box office hit, is revisiting it after criticising the film adaptationEmily Wilson, the first woman to translate Homer’s Odyssey into English, is to retranslate the ancient Greek epic poem from scratch less than a decade after the publication of her acclaimed version.The announcement comes after Wilson attract
entries.content:
Emily Wilson, the first woman to translate Homer’s Odyssey into English, is to retranslate the ancient Greek epic poem from scratch less than a decade after the publication of her acclaimed version.

The announcement comes after Wilson attracted controversy this summer with a scathing assessment of Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster film adaptation of the Odyssey, which she slammed for its “abysmal” writing and lack of sex scenes.

Wilson’s 2017 translation became a bestseller and was praised for making the 3,000-year-old epic poem modern and accessible.

“I’m now retranslating the Odyssey from scratch, with an approach closer to that of my translation of the Iliad, using somewhat more lines than the original, enabling more varied word-length and pacing,” she told the New York Times.

“It’s a complete retranslation. It’s not a revision of the old version,” she told the AP. “I’m about halfway through.”

Nolan cited Wilson’s 2017 translation, including its opening sentence, “Tell me about a complicated man”, as an influence on his adaptation of the poem, released in July this year and starring Tom Holland, Zendaya, Matt Damon and Anne Hathaway.

Nolan’s adaptation took the global box office by storm, making $264m (£196m) during its opening weekend, marking the director’s best ever opening. Book sales saw a huge bump too: UK print sales of the poem increased by 1,400% in the four weeks to 25 July compared with the same period in 2025, after the film’s release in the middle of the month.

Wilson made headlines for her attack on Nolan’s version. Writing in the London Review of Books, she said: “Nolan’s Odyssey lacks many of the elements that make the poem great … The writing is abysmal.”

She continued: “None of the characters has convincing motivation for their actions or words. There are no sex scenes, and all the food looks horrible,” adding, “I would be ashamed to have written any part of this script.”

Her criticism attracted strong reactions, including from novelist Joyce Carol Oates, who accused Wilson of “haughty superiority”.

Wilson’s decision to retranslate the poem predates the row over the film. In an interview recorded in the spring for the ancient-history podcast Instant Classics, she discussed her desire to return to Homer and approach the poem differently from her first translation.

“I’m proud of my Odyssey translation … I think there are lots of good things about the kinds of compression and choices that I was forced into,” Wilson said then.

She has indicated that she will “probably” keep the opening line, “Tell me about a complicated man”. Wilson also added that her original translation relied too heavily on the word “slave”, when more precise terminology could have better reflected the different forms of enslavement depicted in the poem.

The new translation will also give readers far more of Wilson’s scholarly commentary. “I’m also going to quadruple the number of endnotes because endnotes are really fun to write,” she said.

While Wilson’s decision to retranslate Homer’s poem is unusual, it is not without precedent.

“Translators quite often rework or rewrite their own previous translations,” said Matthew Reynolds, professor of English and comparative criticism at Oxford University. “Elizabeth Barrett Browning completely rewrote her translation of Aeschylus’s Prometheus Bound, Ezra Pound repeatedly revised his translations of Guido Cavalcanti, and Yu JongHo (유 종호) translated Jane Eyre into Korean first in 1970 and again in 2004.”

He added: “It shows that translation – especially literary translation – is not just a matter of right or wrong, good or bad, but a continual exploratory process of interpretive reimagining and re-making.”

Wilson’s new Odyssey does not yet have a publication date.

entries.title: Under Story by Chloe Benjamin review – this time-reversal melodrama is quantum hokum
entries.summary: A grieving couple who have lost their son find a way to a mirror universe where time runs backwards – but the narrative machinery is shonky and distractingThere is something farcical – grotesque, even – about life played in reverse. A child falling into a tree. A sandwich emerging from a mouth, bite by reconstituted bite. A doctor unstitching a wound. The world is strange in any order, but rewind
entries.content:
There is something farcical – grotesque, even – about life played in reverse. A child falling into a tree. A sandwich emerging from a mouth, bite by reconstituted bite. A doctor unstitching a wound. The world is strange in any order, but rewind helps us notice – makes the ordinary absurd.

Novels that pick a fight with forward momentum tend to harness this absurdity, revel in it. In The Cockroach (2019), Ian McEwan gives us a sneering Brexit fable about political nostalgia. If voters want to turn back the clock, let them. He unleashes “Economic Reversalism”, which sees employees pay for the privilege of work, and every pound sent back to where it came from. In Time’s Arrow (1991), Martin Amis inverts the Holocaust. Just imagine it, he dares us: a network of sanatoriums instead of death camps. A vast machinery of reparation run by benevolent Nazis. How monstrously laughable.

Joining this backwards bunch is Chloe Benjamin with her third novel, Under Story. It conjures a universe that mirrors our own (a “duoverse”), populated by doppelgangers; a place where the past might be undone, because it hasn’t happened yet.

Here are the fictional facts. In the duoverse, ordinary human life begins underground. Mycelium grow a corpse from rot, like a 3D printer for gizzards. A heart starts beating, for reasons, and a fully grown human crawls up from the soil riddled with elderly ailments, but with a box-fresh brain. Once they’re cleaned up and DNA profiled – the work of “overtakers” – these new/old people are delivered to their children, but in the postal, rather than the obstetric, sense. The doorbell rings.

Brains grow older; bodies grow younger. Cancers unbloom. Cataracts fade. Children raise their parents until they’re spry enough to cope on their own. Nursing homes are convalescent kindergartens. And down at the other end of life, kindergartens are dementia clinics full of geriatric toddlers. Death is birth: neonates are shoved up their mothers in maternity morgues, swallowed by the amniotic dark.

It’s ghoulish stuff, body horror territory: wards of women surgically forced to eat their babies with their hungry vaginas. You might expect – even hope for – some literary depravity: Benjamin Button reimagined by William Burroughs or Agustina Bazterrica. But Under Story is a love story. We follow a forward-born couple, Laurel and Eli, who are grieving their son, Silas. Could a round trip to the duoverse summon him back? Might it also help them to forgive one another? What follows is a 500-page melodrama of parental devotion and quantum hokum. Imagine Orpheus and Eurydice meets Interstellar, but starring Tom Hanks from Big.

Using a combination of speculative physics and prophetic dreams, Laurel and Eli find their way to a portal under the ice of Antarctica and into the duoverse. They adjust quickly to its topsy-turvy logic: September follows October, Obama follows Trump, and the analogue revolution is under way (the record player has just been invented). Handily, the climate is also unravaging – extinct species popping up from the ground like the mushrooms that remade them.

The key to it all is entropy: “this universe moves toward the Big Bang, and entropy is reversed,” Eli explains. He’s a physicist; Laurel is a mycologist. They’ll both do a great deal of explaining.

There can be no life without entropy, but that’s not the problem here. Plenty of imagined worlds are nonsense, and gloriously so. The problem is that Benjamin keeps drawing our attention to her shonky narrative machinery. She answers questions we’d never thought to ask. We learn that “Christmas exists here, even though Jesus won’t be born for two thousand years” and that reverse folks can’t choose to procreate, because the decision is already waiting for them when they grovel out of the placental dirt.

Benjamin’s last novel, 2018’s The Immortalists, was also about foretold lives: four siblings who learn the dates of their deaths from a fortune teller. But the point – and lure – of that novel was doubt. Was the prophecy real or self-fulfilling? Is there a difference? Benjamin left those questions with us. In Under Story, she seems unsure her cosmic premise can carry its own mysteries. But the more we learn, the more distracted we are. And that’s before Benjamin busts out some last-act theatrics – mystical anagrams and fortuitous gadgetry – or subjects us to a death-birth. It’s hard to trust a novel that doesn’t trust itself.

Part of the problem is length. Rewound life is a gimmick, a thought experiment. The books that do it best are wry, incisive and short (the anticlockwise archetype, F Scott Fitzgerald’s The Curious Case of Benjamin Button, is a fleet 40-page story). The longer Laurel and Eli stay in the duoverse, the more contrived it all feels, because the more contrived it has to be. It’s hard to live backwards with dignity, and Benjamin knows it. And so she picks and chooses which bodily functions work in which direction. People walk and talk normally. Have conceptionless sex. Breathe and eat and excrete. It’s entropy galore, except for the life cycle. The author has her backwards cake, and eats it too.

But there are much easier ways to meddle with the past and its sorrows (see Scott Alexander Howard’s The Other Valley or Aja Gabel’s Lightbreakers), which makes all of Benjamin’s picking and choosing feel particularly gruesome. Her duoverse has been elaborately rigged to produce a scene of filial reunion. She has violated the laws of physics, reanimated the dead and turned women’s bodies into tombs all in order to weaponise parental grief.

It’s meant to make us weep, to rouse mighty questions about ageless love, free will and our intimate connection to the planet. But here are some of the questions I scribbled in the margins of Under Story: if every fossil is a future creature, are palaeontologists dino-killers? Will the suffragettes fight to relinquish the vote? If vaginas work backwards, are penises the same: meaty little vacuum cleaners, hoovering up sperm? Once you’ve written a line like that you know your suspension of disbelief has well and truly snapped. And maybe something else has too.
